Este documento consolida o fluxo de inicialização da aplicação e o fluxo de abertura de projeto, desde o boot até o Workspace pronto para uso. É a especificação operacional que conecta a arquitetura (project.md) à implementação real.

1. Fluxo de Inicialização da Aplicação (Boot)
text
1. CranioZ inicia
        ↓
2. Carrega configurações
        ↓
3. Obtém o Project Root
   C:\Users\<user>\Documents\CranioZ\Projects
        ↓
4. Project Catalog lista os projetos
        ↓
5. Home Page exibe a lista
1.1 Detalhamento
Passo 1 — CranioZ inicia
text
main.py
   │
   ├── bootstrap application
   ├── initialize dependency container
   ├── initialize logging
   └── initialize event bus
Passo 2 — Carrega configurações
text
ConfigurationLoader.load()
   │
   ├── read config/app.json
   │       ├── language
   │       ├── theme
   │       ├── recent_projects_limit
   │       └── ...
   ├── read config/paths.json
   │       ├── project_root
   │       ├── flows_root
   │       └── cache_root
   └── read config/user.json
           ├── user_id
           ├── preferences
           └── ...
Passo 3 — Obtém o Project Root
O ProjectPathResolver é inicializado com o root vindo da configuração.

text
ProjectPathResolver.initialize(project_root)
   │
   ├── default: C:\Users\<user>\Documents\CranioZ\Projects
   └── override: config/paths.json → project_root
Regras:

O Project Root é resolvido uma vez no boot e permanece estável durante a sessão.

Se o diretório não existir, é criado com a estrutura mínima.

Se não for acessível, a aplicação falha com erro claro (ProjectRootInaccessible).

Passo 4 — Project Catalog lista os projetos
text
ProjectCatalog.list_projects()
   │
   ├── read <project_root>/info.json
   │       └── se ausente ou corrompido:
   │             └── rebuild_index()
   │                   └── scan <project_root>/*/project.json
   │
   └── return list[ProjectSummary]
Regras:

O Catalog é um read model. Ele não carrega dados clínicos.

Se info.json estiver ausente, o Catalog reconstrói o índice varrendo as pastas.

Se estiver corrompido, o Catalog faz backup e reconstrói.

Passo 5 — Home Page exibe a lista
text
HomePage
   │
   ├── recebe list[ProjectSummary]
   ├── renderiza cards/lista
   ├── habilita busca/filtro
   └── aguarda seleção do usuário
Regras:

A Home Page não acessa o filesystem diretamente.

A Home Page não mantém lista autoritativa própria.

A Home Page apenas exibe o que o Catalog fornece.

2. Fluxo de Abertura de Projeto
text
6. Usuário seleciona um projeto
        ↓
7. Project Manager abre o projeto
        ↓
8. Project Repository carrega project.json
        ↓
9. Project Manager cria o ProjectContext
        ↓
10. Usuário/Project Manager define o Clinical Flow
        ↓
11. ProjectContext + Clinical Flow → Workspace
        ↓
12. Workspace inicializa os módulos do Flow
        ↓
13. Módulos carregam os dados necessários
        ↓
14. Workspace pronta para uso
2.1 Detalhamento
Passo 6 — Usuário seleciona um projeto
text
HomePage
   │
   ├── user clicks project card
   ├── (opcional) user selects clinical flow
   └── emit signal: project_selected(project_id)
Regras:

A seleção é apenas uma intenção. Nada é carregado ainda.

O project_id é o único dado transferido neste passo.

Passo 7 — Project Manager abre o projeto
text
ProjectManager.open_project(project_id)
   │
   ├── check access policy
   │       └── can_open(user, project_id)
   ├── check ProjectInUse
   │       └── se já aberto, retornar contexto existente ou erro
   ├── delegate to ProjectRepository.get(project_id)
   └── build ProjectContext
Regras:

Apenas o Project Manager inicia a abertura.

Verificações de política e concorrência ocorrem antes do carregamento.

Falhas retornam exceções de aplicação (ProjectNotFound, ProjectAccessDenied, ProjectInUse).

Passo 8 — Project Repository carrega project.json
text
ProjectRepository.get(project_id)
   │
   ├── resolve path: <project_root>/<uuid>/
   ├── read project.json
   │       ├── project_id
   │       ├── project_name
   │       ├── patient_id
   │       ├── status
   │       ├── clinical_procedure
   │       ├── schema_version
   │       └── timestamps
   ├── read patient_record.json
   │       ├── patient metadata
   │       ├── medical history
   │       └── logical paths
   ├── read workflow.json
   │       ├── workflow_id
   │       ├── current_step
   │       └── config
   ├── check schema_version
   │       └── se antigo: ProjectMigrationService.migrate()
   └── return Project (domain object)
Regras:

O Repository não decide se o projeto deve ser aberto. Apenas carrega.

Migrações de schema ocorrem aqui, de forma transparente.

Se algum arquivo estiver corrompido, retorna ProjectCorrupted.

Passo 9 — Project Manager cria o ProjectContext
text
ProjectManager.build_context(project)
   │
   ├── extract metadata (read-only)
   ├── extract patient_summary
   ├── extract project_state
   ├── resolve application services
   ├── collect object_references
   └── return ProjectContext
Contrato do ProjectContext:

python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ProjectContext:
    project_id: ProjectId
    metadata: ProjectMetadata          # read-only
    patient_summary: PatientSummary
    project_state: ProjectState
    workflow_id: WorkflowId | None     # pode ser None até seleção
    workflow_config: WorkflowConfig | None
    service_locator: ApplicationServices
    object_references: list[ObjectReference]
Regras:

O ProjectContext é um snapshot de inicialização, não o projeto em si.

É imutável (frozen) para o Workspace.

Não contém caminhos físicos — apenas referências lógicas.

Passo 10 — Define o Clinical Flow
O fluxo pode ser definido de duas formas:

A) Definido pelo usuário na Home Page (antes da abertura):

text
HomePage
   │
   ├── user selects project
   ├── user selects flow
   └── emit signal: project_selected(project_id, flow_id)
B) Resolvido pelo Project Manager (após abertura):

text
ProjectManager.open_project(project_id)
   │
   ├── ...
   ├── WorkflowResolver.resolve(project)
   │       └── determina flow com base em:
   │             ├── project.clinical_procedure
   │             ├── workflow.json (se já houver)
   │             └── preferências do usuário
   └── attach workflow to context
Regras:

A Home Page não implementa lógica de workflow.

O WorkflowResolver é a autoridade de resolução.

Se nenhum flow for resolvido, o Workspace abre em modo "seleção de flow".

Passo 11 — ProjectContext + Clinical Flow → Workspace
text
ProjectManager
   │
   ├── publish ProjectOpened event
   │       └── subscribers: HomePage, Catalog, ...
   │
   └── handoff to Workspace
           │
           │ ProjectContext
           │ + ClinicalFlow
           ▼
       Workspace
Regras:

O handoff é explícito. O Workspace não busca o contexto.

O evento ProjectOpened é publicado para outros subsistemas.

O Workspace se torna o consumidor do contexto.

Passo 12 — Workspace inicializa os módulos do Flow
text
Workspace.initialize(context, flow)
   │
   ├── setup layout
   ├── load flow definition
   │       └── flow.json
   ├── instantiate modules
   │       ├── ImagingModule
   │       ├── SegmentationModule
   │       ├── RegistrationModule
   │       ├── CephalometryModule
   │       └── OsteotomyModule
   ├── inject context into modules
   └── subscribe modules to event bus
Regras:

Os módulos são passivos: recebem o contexto, não o buscam.

Cada módulo é inicializado com o ProjectContext e seu WorkflowConfig.

Módulos podem subscrever eventos relevantes (WorkflowStepChanged, etc.).

Passo 13 — Módulos carregam os dados necessários
text
ImagingModule.initialize(context)
   │
   ├── resolve logical paths via ProjectPathResolver
   │       ├── resolve("imaging/ct")
   │       └── resolve("imaging/cbct")
   ├── load image metadata (não os pixels ainda)
   ├── register with workspace layout
   └── ready

SegmentationModule.initialize(context)
   │
   ├── resolve("segmentation/maxilla")
   ├── load segmentation results (se existirem)
   └── ready

OsteotomyModule.initialize(context)
   │
   ├── resolve("planning/osteotomies")
   ├── load planning data (se existir)
   └── ready
Regras:

Módulos carregam dados sob demanda (lazy loading quando possível).

Módulos nunca constroem caminhos físicos — sempre usam ProjectPathResolver.

Módulos nunca persistem diretamente — sempre usam comandos de aplicação.

Passo 14 — Workspace pronta para uso
text
Workspace
   │
   ├── layout renderizado
   ├── módulos inicializados
   ├── dados carregados (parcialmente)
   ├── event bus ativo
   └── aguardando interação do usuário

Ponto	Falha possível	Tratamento
Boot	ProjectRootInaccessible	Erro fatal com diálogo
Catalog	info.json corrompido	Rebuild index
Catalog	info.json ausente	Rebuild index
Selection	Nenhum projeto	Home Page mostra estado vazio

Modules	Falha ao carregar dados	Módulo mostra estado de erro
7. Regras Arquiteturais Aplicadas
Este fluxo respeita os invariantes definidos em project.md:

✅ Apenas o Project Manager inicia a abertura.

✅ A Home Page é somente-leitura (não escreve, não persiste).

✅ O Project Catalog é um read model.

✅ O Project Repository apenas persiste/recupera.

✅ O ProjectContext é imutável para o Workspace.

✅ O Workspace não busca estado, apenas consome.

✅ Os Módulos são passivos.

✅ Caminhos físicos são resolvidos pelo ProjectPathResolver.

✅ A comunicação entre componentes ocorre via Event Bus.

✅ O Clinical Flow é resolvido pelo WorkflowResolver.

8. Resumo
O fluxo de inicialização e abertura de projeto no CranioZ segue uma sequência clara:

text
BOOT       → configuração, path resolver, catalog
DISCOVERY  → catalog lista, home page exibe
SELECTION  → usuário escolhe projeto (+ flow)
OPENING    → project manager coordena, repository carrega
CONTEXT    → project manager constrói ProjectContext
HANDOFF    → project manager entrega ao workspace
WORKSPACE  → workspace inicializa layout e módulos
MODULES    → módulos carregam dados sob demanda
READY      → workspace pronto para uso
O princípio central é:

A Home Page descobre, o Project Manager coordena, o Repository carrega, o Workspace consome, os Módulos executam.

# Implementation Plan

**Document type:** Roadmap and execution plan
**Status:** Living document
**Scope:** Phased implementation of the CranioZ platform from foundation to release.
**Last updated:** 2026-10-22 (post ADR-0007 to ADR-0012)

---

## 1. Purpose

This document defines the **execution strategy** for building the CranioZ platform. It translates the architectural decisions (ADRs), the domain contracts, and the clinical requirements into a sequenced, testable, and iterative implementation plan.

Its primary goal is to serve as a scientific, technical, and managerial instrument, distinguishing between the strict scope of the PhD research and the long-term evolution of the open-source platform.

---

## 2. Guiding Principles

The implementation follows five strict rules:

1. **Vertical Slices over Horizontal Layers:** We do not build "all models first, then all views". We build a feature from the UI down to the Domain and Persistence, and we test it end-to-end.
2. **No Unresolved Contract Dependencies:** A phase may begin before the previous phase is fully completed, **provided** that the architectural contracts (interfaces, Protocols, ADRs) it depends on are defined, documented, and stable.
3. **Early Persistence:** Persistence is not a final feature. Minimum viable persistence (schema, JSON serialization, repository pattern) must be established from the foundation to prevent architectural rework.
4. **Testable at Every Step:** Every phase ships with its own test suite. The `LayoutBuilder` (pure logic) is tested without Qt. The `LayoutRenderer` is tested with `pytest-qt`. The Domain is tested with pure Python.
5. **Reversible Decisions:** If an architectural decision proves wrong during implementation, it must be caught early and changed without rewriting the entire system.

---

## 3. External Dependencies & Tech Stack

- **Language:** Python 3.12+
- **UI Framework:** PySide6 (Qt 6)
- **3D/Medical Visualization:** VTK, ITK
- **DICOM Parsing:** PyDicom
- **Geometric Modeling:** Open CASCADE (OCCT), CGAL
- **Scientific Computing:** NumPy, SciPy, Numba
- **Persistence:** JSON (Project files, Layout, Scene), SQLite (Professional Module)
- **Testing:** `pytest`, `pytest-qt`, `pytest-benchmark`, `hypothesis`
- **Tooling:** `uv`, `ruff`, `mypy`

---

## 4. Phase Overview

The implementation is divided into 11 phases. These phases are designed to build the *platform* progressively, ensuring the PhD delivers a validated clinical core.

| Phase | Name | Status | Done / Pending |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Phase 0** | Foundation & Boot | ✅ Implemented | — |
| **Phase 1** | Contracts & Core | ✅ Implemented | — |
| **Phase 2** | Workspace | ✅ Implemented | — |
| **Phase 3** | Project & Home Page | ✅ Implemented (core) / 🚧 peripherals pending | Recent Projects, Flow Catalog, Layout persistence pending |
| **Phase 4** | Scene & Visualization | 🚧 In Progress | Contracts ready (ADR-0007, 0008, 0011); implementation pending |
| **Phase 5** | Clinical Flows | ⏳ Planned | Blocked by Phase 4 |
| **Phase 6** | Clinical Pipeline (MVP) | ⏳ Planned | — |
| **Phase 7** | Scientific Validation | ⏳ Planned | — |
| **Phase 8** | Scientific Product (Release 1.0) | ⏳ Planned | — |
| **Phase 9** | Extensibility (Release 2.0) | ⏳ Planned | — |
| **Phase 10**| AI and Nodes (Release 3.0) | ⏳ Planned | — |

**Legend:**
- ✅ Implemented — all deliverables of the phase are in `src/` and tested.
- 🚧 In Progress — the contracts exist and/or the core is in `src/`, but documented deliverables are still missing.
- ⏳ Planned — the phase is blocked by a prior dependency or by an ADR that has not been written.

**Contracts layer.** ADRs 0001–0012 are all written and stable. The contracts for Commands, Scene, Persistence, Layout, Threading, and Telemetry are defined. Phase 4 can now be implemented against them.

---

## 5. Current Focus

**Phase 3 is functionally complete.** The lifecycle core (`ProjectManager`, `ProjectCatalog`), the discovery UI (`HomePage`, `MainWindow`), and the boot wiring are implemented and tested. The peripherals (Recent Projects, Flow Catalog, Layout persistence) are deferred and do not block Phase 4.

**Phase 4 is the active phase.** Its contracts are in place. The next implementation step is the Application layer:

1. **`application/commands/`** — `Command`, `CommandHandler`, `CommandBus`, `CommandDispatcher`, `CommandHandlerRegistry` (ADR-0007). The `CommandBus` is the base for every state mutation; without it, the Scene cannot be mutated and the `ModuleContext.command_bus` is undefined.
2. **`application/tasks/`** — `Task`, `TaskHandle`, `TaskManager`, `CancelToken`, `TaskState` (ADR-0011). Small and isolated.
3. **`application/telemetry/`** — `TelemetrySink`, `Severity`, `MeasurementUnit` (ADR-0012). Small and isolated.
4. **`application/events/`** — `EventSubscription`, `EventPublisher` facade over the existing `EventBus`.
5. **`application/modules/`** — `Module`, `ModuleManifest`, `ModuleContext`, `ModuleRegistry`, `ModuleLoader` (modules.md v10). Aggregates the four above.

Then the Domain:

6. **`domain/scene/`** — `Scene`, `DomainObjectStore` (ADR-0008).
7. **`infrastructure/rendering/`** — `RenderingAdapter`, VTK bridge.
8. **`ui/editors/`** — `Viewport3DEditor`, `MPRViewerEditor`.

### 5.1 Immediate priorities (in order)

1. **Application layer contracts.** Implement `application/commands/`, `application/tasks/`, `application/telemetry/`, `application/events/`, `application/modules/` as Protocols + reference implementations (in-memory) + contract tests. This is the prerequisite for the `ModuleContext` and `ModuleLoader` to exist in code.
2. **Domain `Scene`.** Implement `domain/scene/` per ADR-0008 and `scene.md`.
3. **Rendering bridge.** Implement `RenderingAdapter` and the first concrete Editors (`Viewport3DEditor`, `MPRViewerEditor`).
4. **Boot wiring for the new services.** Update `__main__.py` to construct `TaskManager`, `TelemetrySink`, and `ModuleRegistry`, and inject them into `MainWindow` → `Workspace` → `EditorContext`.

### 5.2 What blocks Phase 4

No blockers remain. The ADRs (0007 Commands, 0008 Scene, 0009 Persistence, 0011 Threading) and the documents (`commands.md`, `scene.md`, `modules.md`) are stable. The only prerequisites are implementation of the Application layer contracts, which is tracked under §5.1 item 1.

### 5.3 Deferred to later phases

- **Recent Projects** (Phase 8): read-only projection, low impact.
- **Flow Catalog** (Phase 5, Bloco 9): depends on `modules.md` (now stable) and on the `WorkflowEngine`.
- **Layout State Persistence** (Phase 5): `layout_state.py`, `layout_io.py`, `overlay_state.py` are stubs; implementation follows ADR-0010.
- **Module-owned persisted state** (Phase 9): deferred until the first module needs it (see `modules.md` v10 §15).

---

## 7. Testing Strategy & Metrics

Testing is a clinical requirement. Metrics must be contextualized to avoid false positives or hardware dependencies.

### 7.1 Coverage Metrics

- **Domain Layer:** High coverage of critical business rules, with 100% of invariants and relevant error cases tested.
- **Application Layer:** Critical command paths and transaction rollbacks tested; contract tests for every Protocol (`ProjectRepository`, `CommandBus`, `TaskManager`, `TelemetrySink`, `ModuleRegistry`, `ModuleLoader`).
- **UI Layer:** 80% coverage of `ui/workspace/`.

### 7.2 Performance Metrics (Reference Hardware)

All performance metrics must be measured against a defined **Reference Dataset** and **Reference Hardware** (e.g., the workstations specified in the PhD infrastructure plan).

- **DICOM Import:** Load a reference dataset of 500 slices in < 10 seconds (including indexing and readiness for first visualization).
- **Rendering:** 30+ FPS for a mesh of 1,000,000 polygons.
  - *Metrics separated into:* Scene update time, GPU upload time, render time.
- **Memory:** < 4 GB RAM during standard facial CT processing.

### 7.3 GPU vs. CPU

- **Correction:** Semantic clinical data belongs to main memory (RAM) and the Domain `Scene`.
- The GPU should only hold **renderable representations** (VTK actors, shaders).
- Use caches and incremental transfer to reduce copies. Do not keep the entire clinical dataset on the GPU.

### 7.4 Concurrency

- **Correction:** `QTimer` is for UI scheduling, not asynchronous execution.
- **TaskManager:** Application layer abstraction for tasks (ADR-0011).
- **Execution:** Heavy CPU-bound tasks must use `QThreadPool`/`QtConcurrent` or `ProcessPool` (for GIL-independent execution), coordinated by the `TaskManager`.
- **Telemetry:** Every long operation must emit `task.dispatch`, `task.complete`, `task.cancel`, or `task.failure` through the `TelemetrySink` with a correlation id (ADR-0012).

---

## 8. Release Criteria (Definition of Done)

A phase is "Done" when:

1. Code is implemented according to the architecture documents.
2. Unit, Widget, and Integration tests are written and passing.
3. Contract tests for every new Protocol exist (a reference in-memory implementation + the same suite for the concrete adapter).
4. The CI pipeline is green.
5. Documentation is updated (including ADRs if a new decision was made).
6. The feature is usable end-to-end by the UI (no orphaned backend code).
7. No `TODO` comments are left without a linked GitHub Issue.

### 8.1 The PhD Deliverable (Release 1.0)

The PhD concludes with the delivery of the validated clinical core. It **does not** include Plugins, Nodes, AI/MCP, or multi-monitor support. These are explicitly deferred to Releases 2.0 and 3.0, demonstrating the platform's long-term vision and extensibility without compromising the thesis deadline.

---

## 9. Summary

By following this roadmap, the CranioZ project ensures that the architectural foundation (Workspace, Commands, Scene) is built correctly before the heavy clinical lifting begins. It respects the scientific validation timelines, protects the PhD scope from feature creep, and establishes a clear path for post-doctoral open-source evolution.

**Post ADR-0007–0012:** All contracts for Phase 4 (Commands, Scene, Persistence, Layout, Threading, Telemetry) are in place. Phase 3 is functionally complete. The next implementation step is the Application layer (`application/commands/`, `application/tasks/`, `application/telemetry/`, `application/events/`, `application/modules/`), which turns the contracts into the wiring that the Scene and the Editors will use.

# Architecture Overview

# 1. Purpose

This document provides a high-level overview of the CranioZ system architecture. It defines the principal architectural concepts, boundaries, responsibilities, and relationships between the major parts of the system.

The purpose is to establish a common architectural vocabulary and provide a reference for developing the core platform, UI, clinical modules, plugins, and infrastructure.

Detailed architectural decisions are documented separately as Architecture Decision Records (ADRs).

# 2. Architectural Goals

The CranioZ architecture is designed to:

- Provide a professional software platform for cranio-maxillofacial surgical planning.
- Separate clinical concepts from generic computational and graphical infrastructure.
- Evolve through independent modules and plugins.
- Keep the core platform small, stable, and reusable.
- Favor Python as the primary implementation language.
- Reuse mature open-source libraries rather than reimplementing established functionality.
- Support multiple clinical workflows without coupling the core to a specific procedure.
- Maintain explicit boundaries between domain logic, application orchestration, infrastructure, and presentation.
- Support deterministic operations, validation, undo/redo, and controlled state changes.
- Provide mechanisms for long-running operations without blocking the UI.
- Provide a stable foundation for automation and AI/MCP integration.
- Support reliable persistence, migration, and backward compatibility.
- Provide architectural foundations for security, auditing, and regulatory requirements.


# 3. Architectural Principles

### 3.1 Domain-first design

Clinical and scientific concepts are represented explicitly in the domain model: Patient, Project, Scene, Mesh, Volume, Landmark, Bone, Maxilla, Mandible, Tooth, Osteotomy, Surgical Guide, Plate, Cephalometric Landmark, Registration, Planning Operation.

Generic computational structures must not be forced to carry clinical semantics that do not belong to them.

### 3.2 Separation of responsibilities

The system is divided into four principal layers: Domain, Application, Infrastructure, and UI. Modules and plugins extend these layers through defined contracts.

The Domain defines concepts and fundamental rules. The Application coordinates operations, state changes, transactions, and workflows. Infrastructure provides technical implementations. The UI presents application capabilities to the user.

### 3.3 Composition over monolithic functionality

CranioZ is not a single large application. The platform provides a stable core; clinical functionality is composed from modules and plugins.

An orthognathic workflow may compose: Tomography → Models → Cephalometry → Registration → Osteotomy → Splint. Another workflow may use a different sequence. The same module may participate in multiple workflows.

### 3.4 Clinical semantics over generic abstractions

A Mesh represents geometric data. A Mandible represents a clinical concept that may reference or contain geometric representations. The same geometric infrastructure supports different clinical entities without making geometry responsible for clinical meaning.

### 3.5 Stable core, extensible edge

The core platform remains intentionally small and stable. New functionality is preferentially implemented through modules, plugins, tools, services, data types, workflows, UI components, and public extension points.

### 3.6 Explicit operations

User-triggered operations are represented explicitly rather than hidden inside UI callbacks:

```text
User → Tool → Command → Application Service → Domain → State Change → Event → UI
```

This provides explicit boundaries for undo/redo, validation, transactions, logging, automation, workflow execution, testing, and AI integration.

### 3.7 UI is not the domain
The UI must not contain clinical rules or core computational logic. UI components present state, collect input, and delegate operations to the Application and Domain layers.

### 3.8 Explicit architectural boundaries
CranioZ follows a Ports and Adapters approach. The Application layer defines ports for persistence, project loading and saving, external computation, rendering integration, and task execution. Infrastructure provides concrete adapters. The Domain remains independent of infrastructure implementations.

## 4. High-Level Architecture
The diagram below represents logical responsibilities, not a strict runtime dependency graph. The vertical arrangement does not represent dependency order.

```
text
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         CranioZ                           │
│                                                           │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │                       UI Layer                      │  │
│  │  Areas · Editors · Toolbars · Overlays              │  │
│  │  Depends on Application for operations              │  │
│  └───────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘  │
│                          │ depends on                     │
│  ┌───────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │                  Application Layer                  │  │
│  │ Commands · Services · Tasks · Flows · Events        │  │
│  │ State · Transactions · Application Ports            │  │
│  └───────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘  │
│                          │ coordinates                    │
│  ┌───────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │                     Domain Layer                    │  │
│  │ Objects · Anatomy · Geometry · Imaging · Planning   │  │
│  │ Scene · Project · Patient · Cephalometry · Units    │  │
│  │ Independent of all infrastructure                   │  │
│  └───────────────────────▲─────────────────────────────┘  │
│                          │ implements contracts           │
│  ┌───────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │                 Infrastructure Layer                │  │
│  │ VTK · ITK · DICOM · OCCT · CGAL · File I/O          │  │
│  │ Adapters for Application/Domain contracts           │  │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                           │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │              Modules / Plugins (transversal)        │  │
│  │  Clinical capabilities and platform extensions      │  │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Infrastructure is orthogonal, not inferior. Modules and Plugins are transversal extensions, not a fifth layer.

## 5. Core Architectural Layers
### 5.1 Domain
The domain layer contains the conceptual model. It must be independent of Qt, VTK, file formats, database implementations, OS APIs, rendering implementations, and external services.

```
text
domain/
├── objects/
├── anatomy/
├── geometry/
├── imaging/
├── scene/
├── project/
├── patient/
├── planning/
├── cephalometry/
├── flow/           # conceptual model of Flows (structure, steps, requirements)
├── nodes/
├── units/
└── parametric_facial_model/
```

domain/flow/ contains the conceptual model of Flows. The execution engine belongs to the Application layer. The definitions are stored in versioned JSON. The progress is persisted in project state.

### 5.2 Application
The application layer coordinates system operations: Commands, command execution, undo/redo, application services, tasks, event dispatch, workflow execution, workflow requirement evaluation and step transitions, application state, transaction boundaries, coordination between modules, validation orchestration, and application ports.

Its primary responsibility is orchestration, not a second domain model.

### 5.3 Infrastructure
The infrastructure layer contains technical implementations: DICOM access, STL/OBJ import and export, VTK/ITK integration, PyDicom, NumPy, Open CASCADE, CGAL, rendering, persistence, serialization, and platform integration.

Implementations must be replaceable when practical. The Domain must not know whether a mesh is internally represented using VTK, OpenMesh, or another library.

The UI layer contains the graphical interface. It presents application state and collects user interaction.

Conceptual UI elements include:

* Application Menu
* Home Page — project table with actions, filters, and application-level icons
* Splash Screen — CranioZ startup screen
* Configurações Iniciais — first-run wizard
* Workspace
* Top Bar — structural component of the Workspace (see §18)
* Areas — structural containers that host Editors
* Editors — functional units hosted inside Areas
* Toolbars — internal to each Editor, declared and materialized by the Editor itself
* Overlays — floating layers managed by the Workspace, including the shared steps_panel
* Dialog and modal windows
* Application settings screens

Area and Editor are distinct concepts
In CranioZ, Area and Editor are distinct but complementary concepts:

An Area is a structural container provided by the Workspace. It occupies a position in the Area Layout Tree and provides the space where Editors are hosted.

An Editor is a functional unit provided by the system, a Module, or a Plugin. It provides a specific interaction experience (Viewport3D, MPR Viewer, Console, Properties, etc.).

Terminology: Area emphasizes where (position, structure); Editor emphasizes what (function, experience).

Area hosts Editors
An Area hosts one or more Editors. The Central Area may be split horizontally and vertically, hosting multiple Editors simultaneously in an internal Editor Layout Tree (the same N-ary split tree model used by the Area Layout Tree).
```
text
Area Central
└── Editor Layout Tree
    Split(HORIZONTAL)
    ├── Split(VERTICAL)
    │   ├── Leaf(editor.mpr_axial)
    │   └── Leaf(editor.mpr_sagittal)
    └── Split(VERTICAL)
        ├── Leaf(editor.mpr_coronal)
        └── Leaf(editor.viewport_3d)
```
The Area provides methods to add, remove, and activate Editors. The Area does not know what an Editor does.

Toolbar is internal to the Editor
A Toolbar is an internal widget of an Editor, not an Area. Each Editor declares and materializes its own Toolbar(s) inside its own content area. An Editor may declare more than one Toolbar, with independent orientations (HORIZONTAL or VERTICAL).

The Workspace never hosts Toolbars. An Area never owns a Toolbar. The Area hosts Editors; the Editors host their Toolbars. This preserves the Workspace's single rule (§1.2): if something is not an Area and not an Overlay, the Workspace does not interpret it.
```
text
Editor
├── Toolbar (Vertical)
│   └── Tools
├── Content
├── Overlays
└── Toolbar (Horizontal)
    └── Tools
```
There is no separate EditorHost
There is no EditorHost abstraction. An Area manages its Editors directly, using its internal Editor Layout Tree. The Area provides the operations needed to host, activate, and remove Editors; the EditorRegistry provides the operations needed to resolve editor_id to concrete Editor types and create instances.

Relationship summary

```text
Workspace
├── Top Bar (Painel Superior)   ← structural component
│   ├── Left segment   — Menu, Home link, toggle Left
│   ├── Center segment — module tabs, + button
│   └── Right segment  — Extras, toggle Right, window controls
│
├── Area Layout Tree
│   ├── Area LEFT      → Editor Layout Tree
│   ├── Area CENTRAL   → Editor Layout Tree (may be split H/V)
│   ├── Area RIGHT     → Editor Layout Tree
│   └── Area BOTTOM    → Editor Layout Tree
│
└── Overlays
    └── steps_panel
```
* The Workspace manages Areas and Overlays.
* An Area hosts Editors and organizes them in its internal Editor Layout Tree.
* An Editor provides a functional experience and materializes its own Toolbars.
* A Toolbar presents Tools inside an Editor.
* A Tool represents an action or interaction mode, defined independently in the ToolRegistry.

Compliance with the single rule
The Workspace manages Areas and Overlays. It does not own clinical state, Tools, Toolbars, or Module behavior. Toolbars, Tools, and Editors are invisible to the Workspace. The Workspace may use platform services (LayoutRenderer, EditorRegistry, OverlayManager) to materialize and manage its elements, but it does not interpret them.

## 6. Module Composition
A module represents a coherent functional capability. Modules do not own or implement the fundamental UI infrastructure. They compose their functionality using platform-provided primitives and extension points.

A module may compose: Tools, Commands, Services, Data Types, Editors, Toolbars, Flows, and Capabilities.

Declared vs materialized
The contract between module and platform is:

The module declares its desired composition in a ModuleUISpec.

The platform validates the declaration.

The Workspace creates or reuses Areas and resolves the declared Editors.

The Workspace applies the composition to the LayoutTree.

Layout state may be personalized by the user and persisted with the project.

The initial composition declared by the module is distinct from the active layout, which may have been personalized. Activation of a module must not overwrite a saved personalized layout.

Semantic regions
```
text
Orthognathic Module
      │
      ▼
ModuleUISpec (Workspace Composition)
      │
      ├── LEFT      → Lists
      │                (Object List, Cephalometric Points, Masks)
      ├── CENTRAL   → Editing Area
      │                (3D Viewport, MPR Viewer)
      ├── RIGHT     → Auxiliary Tools
      │                (Properties, Material, Osteotomy Patterns)
      └── BOTTOM    → Consoles and Extras
                       (Console, History, AI Assistant)
```

The regions LEFT, CENTRAL, RIGHT, and BOTTOM are semantic conventions used by the module to declare its initial composition. They are not fixed positions imposed on the user.

The Workspace layout is an N-ary tree of splits. The semantic regions guide the LayoutBuilder in constructing the initial tree. Once built, the user may move, resize, hide, or add Areas.

Separation between platform and module
```
text
Platform
    ├── Areas (host Editors)
    ├── Editors
    ├── Toolbars (internal to Editors)
    ├── Tools
    ├── Commands
    ├── Overlays (including steps_panel)
    └── Layout mechanism (N-ary tree of splits)
```
The module declares which Areas exist and which Editors occupy them. It does not declare Toolbars directly; the Toolbars are declared by the Editors the module selects. The module does not declare Overlays, the layout mechanism, or other modules.

A module is a consumer and composer of platform capabilities, not an owner of the underlying UI infrastructure.

## 7. Module Contract
A module may expose or register:

```
text
Module
├── Module Specification
├── Lifecycle
├── State
├── Tools
├── Commands
├── Services
├── Data Types
└── Capabilities
```
The module contract defines identity, lifecycle, dependencies, registration, public capabilities, extension points, state ownership, resource management, and compatibility requirements. The detailed contract is defined in a dedicated document and ADR.

## 8. Flows
A Flow represents an ordered sequence of steps to accomplish a task. Each step is associated with one module by default. A flow may reuse the same module in multiple steps.
```
text
Orthognathic Planning
  Step 1: Tomography   → tomography_module
  Step 2: Models       → models_module
  Step 3: Cephalometry → cephalometry_module
  Step 4: Registration → registration_module
  Step 5: Osteotomy    → osteotomy_module
  Step 6: Splint       → splint_module
```
Flows orchestrate. They do not implement clinical logic. The Flow declares:

Ordered steps and associated modules

Requirements (referencing registered validators)

Actions (referencing registered handlers)

Completion criteria and dependencies

Contextual actions and workflow configuration

Versioned user-facing labels and resource references

Identifiers in the JSON refer to implementations registered by the application. Unknown identifiers are configuration errors, not silently ignored.

The Python workflow engine belongs to the Application layer. It loads and validates the JSON, evaluates requirements, calculates step state, and determines the next step. When a step is completed, it asks the application to activate the module for the next step.

The steps_panel is a shared Overlay hosted by the Workspace. It presents the unified step list across module changes, sends user actions to the workflow engine, and displays progress. It is not an Area.

Flow definitions and case progress are separate. JSON stores the versioned definition; the project stores the active step, completion status, choices, and references.

Failure handling:

If a requirement is unmet, the step remains in blocked state.

If a module is unavailable, the engine reports a configuration error.

If a Flow definition was updated since the project was saved, the engine resolves against the version stored with the project, not the latest version.

Flows can be created, edited, removed, exported, and imported through Gerir Fluxos.

## 9. Tools, Commands, Services, and Tasks
Tool. An operational capability exposed to the user. A Tool does not necessarily contain the implementation.

Command. An executable application operation. Every state-changing operation passes through the Command mechanism.

Each Command declares:

Whether it is reversible (undo/redo) or requires a compensating action

Its transaction requirements

Its authorization requirements

The events it publishes on success

The Command mechanism ensures that all state-changing operations follow a consistent path. It does not automatically guarantee reversibility, atomicity, or authorization — those are declared in each Command's contract.

Service. Reusable application or domain functionality not naturally belonging to a single entity. Services have explicit contracts.

Task. A potentially long-running operation managed by the Application layer. Provides execution, progress, cancellation, error propagation, result delivery, and state reporting.

## 10. Transactions and State Consistency
Multi-step operations must not leave the project in an invalid intermediate state.
```
text
Command → Transaction Boundary → Domain Changes → Commit → Events
```

Not all infrastructure operations are transactional by nature. Changes to memory, files, and other resources may require different commit and recovery strategies.

For operations that cannot be reverted automatically, the Command contract specifies the compensation or recovery mechanism.

## 11. Concurrency and Long-Running Operations
Potentially long-running operations must be executed outside the UI event loop.

The GIL is not the architectural reason: VTK, ITK, and Open CASCADE release the GIL during native operations.

text
UI → Tool → Command → Task → Application Service → Domain / Infrastructure → Progress / Result / Error → Event → UI
Modules must not independently reinvent the concurrency model.

## 12. Scene and Rendering Architecture
The Domain Scene represents semantic state. The visualization backend (VTK) represents that state graphically. These representations must not become independent sources of truth.
```
text
Domain Scene → Application Events → Visualization Adapter → VTK Scene / Render Window
```

The Domain does not depend directly on VTK. A visualization adapter translates domain state into renderer-specific representations. The VTK representation remains an implementation detail.

## 13. Event Architecture
text
Tool → Command → Domain / Service → State Change → Event → Subscribers
Commands express that something should happen. Events communicate that something happened.

Events are published only after successful commit. A rolled-back transaction must not publish success events.

Events must not be used as hidden commands. The Event Bus must not cause the Domain to depend on the UI or rendering system.

## 14. Data Architecture
The system works with Volumes, Meshes, Images, Landmarks, Anatomical Structures, Teeth, Surgical Plans, Osteotomies, Plates, Guides, Patient Information, and Project Information. Technical representations may include DICOM, STL, OBJ, JSON, image arrays, VTK data structures, and Open CASCADE structures.

14.1 Objects and DataTypes
An Object provides common identity and metadata. A DataType defines a stable type recognized by the platform.

Complete contracts for Object identity, lifecycle, registration, and serialization are defined in dedicated documents.

## 15. Persistence
CranioZ projects require a versioned semantic project representation, distinguishing between: semantic project metadata, object identity and relationships, configuration and state, large binary data, and domain-specific formats.

The persistence architecture addresses schema versioning, migration, stable object identifiers, backward compatibility, deterministic serialization, integrity of references, separation of metadata and large data, and error recovery.

Persisted case or project state includes workflow progress needed to resume work: workflow definition version, active step, completion state, and stable references.

## 16. Dependency Architecture
CranioZ follows a Ports and Adapters approach.
```
text
UI → Application Ports → Domain
```
Contracts are owned by the layer that defines them:

Domain contracts represent domain concepts.

Application ports represent application-level dependencies, implemented by Infrastructure.

Infrastructure adapters implement Application ports.

The Domain must not depend on infrastructure implementations.

## 17. Plugin Architecture and API Stability
A plugin may provide: Modules, Tools, Services, Data Types, UI components, Flows, Capabilities, and Integrations.

Plugins communicate through public APIs and extension points, not private implementation details.

Public extension points are versioned: module contracts, tool contracts, command contracts, service interfaces, DataType registration, flow definitions, UI extension points, plugin manifests, event contracts, and capability interfaces.

The plugin system distinguishes Public API, Internal API, and Experimental API. Plugins declare their compatibility requirements.

## 18. Workspace and UI Composition
The Workspace provides the environment in which modules and their UI components operate.

Structure and Overlays
The Workspace has two distinct structural categories:
```
text
Workspace
├── Top Bar (Painel Superior)   ← structural component
│   ├── Left segment   — Menu, Home link, toggle Left
│   ├── Center segment — module tabs, + button
│   └── Right segment  — Extras, toggle Right, window controls
│
├── Area Layout Tree
│   ├── Area LEFT      → Editor Layout Tree
│   ├── Area CENTRAL   → Editor Layout Tree (may be split H/V)
│   ├── Area RIGHT     → Editor Layout Tree
│   └── Area BOTTOM    → Editor Layout Tree
│
└── Overlays
    └── steps_panel
```
Structural components are part of the Workspace itself. They have a fixed position and are not repositionable or closeable by the user.

Overlays are floating layers managed by the Workspace. They can be moved, resized, and closed. The steps_panel is the primary example.

Top Bar ownership
The Top Bar is a structural component of the Workspace, not an Overlay and not a MainWindow component.

The MainWindow is only the operating system frame. The Home Page has its own structural header (the home top bar with community actions), separate from the Workspace Top Bar.

The distinction matters:

Aspect	Top Bar	steps_panel
Category	Structural	Overlay
Position	Fixed at top	Repositionable
Lifecycle	Workspace	Active Flow
Movable	No	Yes
Closeable	No	Yes
Resizable	No	Yes
The Home Page and the Workspace each have their own structural header and their own overlays. Neither belongs to the MainWindow.

The steps_panel presents the active Flow across module boundaries. A module may contribute Areas and Editors to the Workspace (via its ModuleUISpec), while the steps_panel remains visible. The Editors hosted in those Areas declare their own Toolbars and reference Tools from the ToolRegistry.

## 19. Clinical Semantics and Geometry
A fundamental distinction is made between Geometry and Clinical Meaning.

text
Mesh → Anatomical Structure → Mandible
Mesh → Surgical Object → Osteotomy Segment
The geometric representation may be shared, replaced, or transformed without changing the clinical concept.

## 20. Observability and Auditability
Observability includes structured logging, error reporting, metrics, performance measurements, tracing, and diagnostic information.

Observability is distinguished from clinical or security auditing.

Audit mechanisms record actor, timestamp, action, affected object or project, and operation result. Audit requirements depend on the deployment context and applicable regulatory requirements.

## 21. Security and Compliance
CranioZ may process patient-related information and must provide architectural mechanisms for protecting sensitive data.

Security considerations include authentication, authorization, access control, data protection, encryption in transit and at rest, secure storage and data exchange, auditability, sensitive-data handling, and dependency and supply-chain security.

CranioZ captures professional identity information (name, professional license, address) during first-run configuration. This information is used in generated reports and signed clinical documents.

Professional identification, authentication, authorization, and digital signature are separate concerns. A stored signature image is not equivalent to a cryptographic digital signature. Each of these concerns has its own requirements, documented separately according to deployment and regulatory context.

Regulatory requirements depend on the deployment context, jurisdiction, intended use, and regulatory classification. Relevant frameworks may include LGPD, applicable ANVISA requirements, HIPAA, and MDR.

## 22. Automation and MCP
Automation is an extension of the existing architecture, not a separate execution model.

CranioZ treats AI as a first-class citizen. The AIAssistantEditor is a regular Editor presented in the Bottom Area. AI executes commands through the same Command mechanism used by human-triggered Tools.
```
text
AI / MCP → Tool / Command / Service → Application → Domain → State
```
Every AI-executed command is auditable (via AuditLog) and visible in the History Editor. Reversibility depends on the specific Command contract. Commands declare whether they support undo/redo or require a compensating action.

AI does not bypass the Application and Domain layers, and is subject to the same validation, authorization, and audit rules as human-triggered commands.

## 23. Testing and Validation
Tests follow architectural boundaries and account for the numerical and geometric nature of the system.

Domain tests validate entities, rules, clinical semantics, mathematical calculations, and invariants.

Application tests validate commands, services, tasks, flows, events, state transitions, and transaction boundaries.

Infrastructure tests validate file I/O, DICOM handling, serialization, external library adapters, rendering integration, and persistence.

UI tests validate user interaction, view behavior, tool presentation, workspace composition, UI state synchronization, Steps Panel state, and workflow navigation across module changes.

Geometric and numerical validation requires tests that validate properties of the resulting data: mesh validity, watertightness, manifoldness, surface area, volume, normal orientation, topological invariants, distance tolerances, transformation accuracy, landmark preservation, registration error, and numerical stability.

Where appropriate, the test suite uses property-based tests, geometric invariants, numerical tolerance checks, reference datasets, regression datasets, golden results, and visual regression testing.

## 24. Architectural Boundaries
Boundary	Principle
Domain ↔ UI	Domain must not depend on UI
Domain ↔ Qt	Domain should not depend on Qt
Domain ↔ VTK	Domain should not depend directly on VTK
Application ↔ UI	UI invokes application capabilities rather than implementing them
Module ↔ Core	Modules use public platform contracts
Module ↔ Module	Prefer explicit contracts over internal access
Plugin ↔ Core	Plugins use public extension points
Persistence ↔ Domain	Persistence is an implementation concern
Rendering ↔ Domain	Rendering state is derived from semantic application state
AI/MCP ↔ Core	AI executes Commands through the same unified entry point as human tools
Long-running Work ↔ UI	Computational tasks must not block the UI event loop


## 25. Architectural Invariants
The UI event loop must remain responsive.

Potentially long-running operations must use the Application task mechanism.

The Domain layer must not depend on Qt, VTK, or infrastructure implementations.

The Domain Scene is the semantic source of truth for scene state.

Renderer-specific state must be derived from or synchronized with application/domain state.

Multi-step state-changing operations must have explicit transaction boundaries.

Modules must use standardized application mechanisms for long-running operations.

Plugins must use public extension points rather than internal implementation details.

Public plugin APIs must be versioned and compatibility must be explicit.

Events communicate state changes and are published only after successful commit.

Persistence must support schema evolution and migration.

Numerical and geometric operations must be validated using appropriate tolerances and invariants.

Security-sensitive operations must have explicit authorization boundaries.

Clinical or audit-relevant actions should be traceable where required.

Rendering infrastructure must remain replaceable without redefining the domain model.

26. Project Structure
```
text
cranioz/
├── .github/
├── src/
│   └── cranioz/
│       ├── domain/
│       ├── application/
│       ├── infrastructure/
│       ├── ui/
│       ├── modules/
│       ├── config/              # system configuration (defaults)
│       ├── settings/            # user preferences (logic)
│       └── assets/
├── plugins/
├── tests/
├── docs/
├── examples/
├── scripts/
├── pyproject.toml
├── README.md
├── LICENSE
├── CHANGELOG.md
├── CONTRIBUTING.md
└── CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md
```
Config vs Settings:

config/ — system configuration. Describes how the system works. Defined by developers/admins. Rarely changed. Versioned with the software.

settings/ — user preferences. Describes what the user chose. Defined by the user through the UI. Frequently changed. Persisted outside the package (e.g., ~/.cranioz/settings/).

The ConfigurationLoader merges defaults from config/ with user overrides from the OS-specific application data directory.

## 27. Architectural Evolution
Early versions prioritize stable domain concepts; core object and DataType infrastructure; application command model; module contracts; UI workspace infrastructure; basic persistence; task execution infrastructure; essential clinical modules; validation and testing infrastructure.

Advanced capabilities are planned for progressive introduction: advanced CAD operations; parametric facial models; finite element analysis; AI-assisted segmentation and planning; MCP integration; advanced automation; third-party plugin ecosystems.

Architectural evolution favors incremental changes over large-scale rewrites. Changes to public contracts are explicitly documented and versioned.

## 28. Architecture Decision Records
Specific architectural decisions are documented under docs/architecture/adr/.

The architecture is expected to have ADRs addressing: programming language and runtime; UI framework; dependency architecture and Ports & Adapters; application transaction boundaries; Unit of Work and rollback; concurrency and task execution; Module Contract / SPI; Plugin API and versioning; DataType registry; command architecture; event system; scene and rendering synchronization; persistence format; project schema versioning and migration; dependency policy; rendering architecture; workflow architecture; workflow definition schema and execution contract; Steps Panel and Workspace integration; Area = Editor; Top Bar ownership; Object Library; Custom Flows; AI command execution; observability; security and auditability; geometric and numerical validation; MCP integration.

The overview.md describes the structure and principles. The ADRs explain why specific decisions were made and the contracts developers will implement.

# Clinical Workflows

## 1. Purpose

A **Clinical Workflow** is a versioned, declarative sequence that guides a user through a clinical task by coordinating steps, requirements, and application modules. It expresses how work is organized without duplicating the clinical functionality implemented by modules.

This document describes workflow concepts, configuration, execution, state, and persistence. The `steps_panel` document describes the reusable UI component that presents a workflow. The Workspace document describes how that panel is hosted as a shared Overlay.

## 2. Core concepts

### 2.1 Workflow

A workflow has a stable identifier, a display name, a version, and an ordered list of steps. JSON is the source format for workflow definitions. A workflow may be provided by the platform, a module, or a plugin, subject to validation and compatibility rules.

### 2.2 Step

A step is a meaningful unit of work in the workflow. Each step has a stable ID and is associated with one module by default. The same module may be used in multiple steps. A step may contain substeps, guidance, input fields, requirements, dependencies, and completion criteria.

The step list is defined once by the workflow and remains unified as the user moves between modules. A step is not itself a module, view, or workspace Area.

### 2.3 Substep

A substep is a more focused action or check within a step, such as orienting a model, importing a data source, reviewing landmarks, or confirming a result. Substeps may have their own instructions, fields, requirements, and state.

### 2.4 Requirement

A requirement is a verifiable condition used to determine whether an action, substep, or step may proceed or be completed. Requirements are mandatory or optional. A mandatory requirement blocks completion while it remains unmet; an optional requirement does not.

Alternative requirements allow more than one valid path to the same outcome. For example, dental arches may be obtained from aligned intraoral scans or segmented from a facial CT. If intraoral scans are selected, their alignment to the CT becomes a requirement for that path.

## 3. Relationship to modules and the Workspace

The workflow engine and module activation belong to the Application layer. The Workspace is not the workflow controller and does not know clinical step semantics.

The usual transition is:

1. The workflow engine determines the active step and its associated module.
2. The Application layer loads or activates that module.
3. The Application layer provides the module's `ModuleUISpec` to the Workspace.
4. The Workspace materializes the specification and preserves its shared `steps_panel` Overlay.
5. The panel displays the updated workflow state and sends user actions back to the application.

When a step is completed, the workflow engine evaluates its requirements. If the completion criteria are met, it persists the transition and asks the application to activate the module for the next step. The Workspace only materializes the resulting module UI specification; it does not decide which module comes next.

By default, one step references one module. This keeps the workflow straightforward to configure and navigate. A module can appear in several steps. A future workflow that genuinely needs one step to coordinate several modules must declare that explicitly and be validated; it must not be inferred from a step's title or position.

## 4. Responsibilities

### JSON workflow definition

The JSON definition declares stable identifiers, order, modules, user-facing content, file-input descriptions, requirement references, dependencies, actions, and completion criteria. It contains data only; it does not contain Python snippets, algorithms, or executable callbacks.

### Python workflow engine

The Python engine:

- loads and validates workflow definitions;
- checks references to modules, validators, and actions against registries/contracts;
- evaluates applicable requirements using application and module results;
- computes workflow, step, and substep states;
- validates user requests to proceed or complete a step;
- requests module activation through the Application layer;
- persists progress and publishes state changes to the UI.

Unknown module, requirement, or action IDs are configuration errors. They must not be silently ignored or treated as satisfied.

### Modules

Modules perform their clinical or technical operations and report verifiable results to the Application layer. They do not own the global step sequence. Module results and data objects are referenced by stable IDs rather than by temporary UI state or local paths.

### `steps_panel`

The shared panel presents the flow, its active step, instructions, requirements, and progress. It sends commands to the application and displays the returned state. It does not evaluate clinical criteria or mark a step complete locally. Visual behavior and accessibility requirements are specified in `steps_panel.md`.

## 5. JSON definition

Workflow definitions are stored as versioned JSON files. The JSON sequence is the source of step order. A definition may include:

- workflow ID, name, version, and description;
- ordered steps and their module IDs;
- optional substeps;
- titles, descriptions, instructional text, captions, and image references;
- file-input declarations;
- requirement IDs and mandatory/optional status;
- alternative satisfaction paths;
- dependencies between steps;
- contextual action IDs and completion criteria.

The Python engine validates each definition against a schema before execution. It checks unique IDs, valid module and action references, dependency references, dependency cycles, supported field types, and resource references.

### 5.1 Example

The following example shows a mandatory CT, optional intraoral scans, and two valid ways to meet the mandatory dental-arches requirement.

```json
{
  "id": "orthognathic_planning",
  "name": "Orthognathic Planning",
  "version": 1,
  "steps": [
    {
      "id": "patient_data",
      "title": "Patient Data",
      "module": "patient_data_module",
      "description": "Select the data to be used for planning.",
      "file_inputs": [
        {
          "id": "face_ct",
          "label": "Facial CT",
          "type": "file",
          "required": true,
          "accepted_formats": [".dcm", ".nii.gz"],
          "multiple": true,
          "import_action": "import_face_ct"
        },
        {
          "id": "intraoral_scans",
          "label": "Intraoral scans",
          "type": "file",
          "required": false,
          "accepted_formats": [".stl", ".ply", ".obj"],
          "multiple": true,
          "import_action": "import_intraoral_scans"
        }
      ],
      "guidance": [
        {
          "type": "text",
          "text": "A facial CT is required. Dental arches may come from aligned intraoral scans or segmentation of the CT."
        },
        {
          "type": "image",
          "src": "assets/patient_data_guide.svg",
          "alt": "The data sources used for planning.",
          "caption": "Planning inputs"
        }
      ],
      "requirements": [
        {
          "id": "face_ct_available",
          "required": true,
          "check": "case_has_face_ct"
        },
        {
          "id": "dental_arches_available",
          "required": true,
          "satisfy_any": [
            "intraoral_scans_aligned",
            "dental_arches_segmented_from_ct"
          ]
        },
        {
          "id": "selected_scans_aligned",
          "required": true,
          "when": "intraoral_scans_selected",
          "check": "intraoral_scans_aligned"
        }
      ],
      "completion": {
        "all_required_satisfied": true
      }
    },
    {
      "id": "cephalometry",
      "title": "Cephalometry",
      "module": "cephalometry_module",
      "depends_on": ["patient_data"],
      "description": "Acquire and review cephalometric landmarks.",
      "requirements": [
        {
          "id": "landmarks_reviewed",
          "required": true,
          "check": "cephalometry_points_reviewed"
        }
      ],
      "completion": {
        "all_required_satisfied": true
      }
    },
    {
      "id": "osteotomy",
      "title": "Osteotomies",
      "module": "osteotomy_module",
      "depends_on": ["cephalometry"],
      "description": "Plan and review the osteotomies.",
      "requirements": [
        {
          "id": "osteotomy_plan_reviewed",
          "required": true,
          "check": "osteotomy_plan_reviewed"
        }
      ],
      "completion": {
        "all_required_satisfied": true
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

The identifiers in `check`, `when`, and `import_action` refer to implementations registered by the Python application. The JSON describes which checks and actions apply; the application code executes them.

File-input declarations describe a selection field and accepted formats. They do not store file contents or authorize arbitrary filesystem access. After user selection, the application validates and imports the files, then records stable references to the managed objects. Temporary session paths are not persisted as object identities.

## 6. Workflow state and transitions

The workflow engine is the authority for state. The UI presents the state it receives and cannot independently mark a step complete.

### 6.1 Step and substep states

| State | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `pending` | Not started. |
| `active` | Currently selected for work. |
| `blocked` | Cannot proceed or complete because a dependency or mandatory requirement is unmet. |
| `completed` | Required substeps and applicable mandatory requirements have been verified. |

Substeps use the same state model. A step is `completed` only when its completion criteria are satisfied. Optional requirements can remain unmet. Normally one step is active at a time; later steps may be blocked by unmet dependencies.

### 6.2 State transitions

```text
pending -> active -> completed
   |         |
   +------> blocked
blocked -> pending or active, when its blocking condition is resolved
completed -> active or blocked, if supporting data changes and criteria no longer hold
```

The engine reevaluates affected requirements when data or module results change. If a completed step becomes invalid, the engine updates the current state and records the reason; it does not erase the prior completion event. A user may return to an earlier step for review according to the workflow's navigation rules.

## 7. Persistence, resumption, and versioning

Workflow definition and per-case progress are separate:

- The versioned JSON file defines the workflow and is not mutated to store user progress.
- Persisted project or case state records the active workflow ID and definition version, active step/substep, requirement status, user choices, and stable references to relevant module objects.

Closing and reopening a case restores its workflow progress, so the user can continue from the saved state. Large CTs, scans, and meshes are managed by the data/persistence architecture; workflow state stores references to them rather than duplicating them.

The persistence model keeps a current progress snapshot for restoration and an event/evidence history for relevant changes, such as starting or completing a step, satisfying or invalidating a requirement, the actor, timestamp, and references supporting the result. Writes must preserve consistency between state and recorded evidence.

Each case remains associated with the workflow definition version under which it began. A new definition version must not silently change the interpretation of an in-progress case. An incompatible change requires retaining the original definition or performing an explicit, validated, and recorded migration.

When multiple users may edit the same case, writes check the version of the state read. Concurrent changes must not be silently overwritten. Before recording step completion, the engine reevaluates requirements against the latest state and reports conflicts that cannot be merged safely.

## 8. Content and resource validation

Workflow JSON may provide user-facing titles, descriptions, instructions, labels, captions, and references to PNG or SVG images. The content is declarative and is never executed as code.

Images belong to a known workflow resource package. Before loading a reference, the validator normalizes the relative path, confirms the resolved file remains inside the allowed package directory, checks its extension and media type against an allowlist, and rejects absolute paths, traversal (`..`), and links escaping the package. Missing or invalid resources produce clear validation errors.

Texts are stored directly in the workflow JSON in the current architecture. If multiple languages are introduced, translation catalogs may refer to stable workflow, step, and substep IDs without changing workflow logic. Catalog versioning is a separate localization decision.

## 9. Workflow execution lifecycle

1. The application loads the workflow JSON and validates its schema and registered references.
2. The engine loads or initializes progress for the project/case and resolves the workflow definition version.
3. The engine determines the active step and asks the application to activate its associated module.
4. The module provides results through application contracts; the Workspace materializes its `ModuleUISpec`.
5. The shared `steps_panel` displays the active flow, current step, guidance, inputs, requirements, and progress.
6. User actions from the panel or module are sent to the engine as application commands.
7. The engine reevaluates requirements, validates requested transitions, persists state and evidence, and publishes updated presentation state.
8. When the step is complete, the engine selects the next eligible step and requests activation of its module.
9. When the project/case is reopened, the engine restores the saved workflow progress and resumes at the appropriate step.

## 10. Orthognathic planning example

An initial orthognathic planning workflow may use this ordered sequence:

1. Patient data — `patient_data_module`
2. Model alignment — `registration_module`
3. Segmentation — `segmentation_module`
4. Cephalometry — `cephalometry_module`
5. Osteotomies — `osteotomy_module`
6. Surgical guide — `surgical_guide_module`

The sequence is illustrative; the JSON definition is authoritative. Each step may contain multiple substeps. For example, Cephalometry may include choosing a reference method, orienting the head, acquiring or reviewing landmarks, and confirming the result. After mandatory criteria are satisfied and the user completes the step, the application activates the next step's module while the same `steps_panel` remains visible.

## 11. Validation and failure handling

Workflow definitions are validated before use. At minimum, validation checks:

- schema and version support;
- unique workflow, step, substep, field, and requirement IDs;
- known module, validator, and action references;
- valid dependency references and absence of dependency cycles;
- supported input field types and file-format declarations;
- resource paths constrained to the workflow package;
- valid completion rules and alternatives.

If a definition is invalid, the application reports the affected workflow and configuration issue clearly and does not execute an incomplete or ambiguous definition. If an individual optional guidance resource is missing, the application reports it and may continue when the resource is not required for safe execution.

## 12. Design principles

- **Declarative configuration:** JSON describes workflow structure and content; Python implements execution.
- **Unified sequence:** a workflow owns one ordered list of steps across module changes.
- **Module composition:** steps normally map to one module; modules do not own the global sequence.
- **Verifiable completion:** mandatory criteria are checked by registered application logic.
- **Flexible paths:** alternatives are explicit and optional requirements do not block valid paths.
- **Resumable cases:** workflow progress is persisted separately from its definition.
- **Traceability:** state changes retain evidence and stable references.
- **Workspace independence:** the Workspace hosts the shared panel and materializes module UI specs without interpreting workflow semantics.
- **Safe resources:** file inputs and image references are validated by the application.
